title: Van Hollen Claims Growing Support in High-Stakes Bid to Oust Schumer as Senate Democratic Leader
snippet: Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen claims momentum in his challenge against Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leadership, warning that the party is currently 'on probation' with American voters.
content:
Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen signaled confidence Sunday in his bid to unseat Chuck Schumer as leader of the Senate Democrats, declaring that momentum is shifting toward a caucus eager for institutional reform.

Appearing on NBC’s "Meet the Press," the Maryland Democrat disclosed that he currently holds "north of 15" votes in his campaign for the top leadership post. While that remains short of the 28 votes required to win the caucus election scheduled for December, Van Hollen insisted he has a clear path to victory over Schumer, the long-serving party leader from New York.

A Party 'On Probation'

"If you look at our caucus, you can see a huge appetite for change," Van Hollen said. "They are seeing the American people and the Democratic Party calling for change. They also want to change the way we do business in the United States Democratic caucus and the United States Senate."

Framing the stakes for Democrats in the upcoming Congress, Van Hollen warned that the party is effectively "on probation" with the electorate and cannot afford complacency. "You don’t earn people’s trust by going back to business as usual," he added.

While Schumer's allies point to past legislative achievements and historic electoral victories under his stewardship, Van Hollen's supporters are pitching him as a reform-minded leader capable of navigating a tough legislative terrain under the incoming Trump administration.

Filibuster Rules and 2028 Ambitions

On legislative mechanics, Van Hollen personally characterized the Senate's 60-vote filibuster threshold as an "anti-democratic provision." While acknowledging that any procedural shifts must reflect caucus consensus, he suggested establishing firm criteria to evaluate alternatives—such as a traditional talking filibuster—if Republicans block high-priority legislation like voting rights or political corruption bills.

Van Hollen also firmly closed the door on a future White House bid. Despite previously weighing a potential presidential run, the senator confirmed he will not run in 2028, opting instead to dedicate his full attention to the Senate.

"After I saw the scope of this victory, this call from the American people, my view is now we have to deliver, we have to earn people’s trust, and that would be my focus entirely," Van Hollen said. "So no, I’m not running for president in 2028."
